prompt: For a binomial count with \(n = {{n}}\) and \(p = {{p}}\), can the normal approximation be used? The rule is \(np > 5\) and \(n(1-p) > 5\).
choices: {{c1}} ;; {{c2}} ;; It depends only on \(n\), which must be at least 30
data: n <- sample(c(8, 10, 12, 15, 20, 30, 40), 1); p <- sample(c(0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.5, 0.7, 0.8), 1); a <- round(n * p, 4); b <- round(n * (1 - p), 4); ok <- a > 5 && b > 5; s1 <- paste0('\\(np = ', a, '\\) and \\(n(1-p) = ', b, '\\)'); yes <- paste('Yes:', s1, 'are both greater than 5'); no <- paste('No:', s1, 'are not both greater than 5'); c1 <- if (ok) yes else no; c2 <- if (ok) no else yes
explanation: Read the rule as two checks joined by 'and': both must pass. \(np\) is the expected number of successes and \(n(1-p)\) the expected number of failures. Note that \(n(1-p)\) means \(n\) times \((1-p)\): work out the bracket first. A value of exactly 5 does not pass, because \(>\) means strictly greater than.

prompt: A binomial count has \(n = {{n}}\) trials and \(p = {{p}}\). For the normal approximation, calculate \(\mu = np\) and \(\sigma = \sqrt{np(1-p)}\). Give \(\sigma\) to 2 decimal places.
explanation: Letters side by side are multiplied: \(np\) is \(n \times p\). Under the square root, \(np(1-p)\) is three things multiplied together: \(n\), \(p\), and \((1-p)\). Work out the bracket, multiply, then take the square root last, because the root's roof covers everything.
worked:
\(\mu = {{n}} \times {{p}} = {{n * p}}\)
\(\sigma = \sqrt{ {{n}} \times {{p}} \times {{1 - p}} } = \sqrt{ {{n * p * (1 - p)}} } = {{round(sqrt(n * p * (1 - p)), 4)}}\)

prompt: Under the null hypothesis, \(p = 0.5\) in \(n = {{n}}\) trials. You observe \(X = {{x}}\) successes. Use the normal approximation \(Pr[X \geq Observed] \approx Pr\left[Z > \dfrac{Observed - \frac{1}{2} - np}{\sqrt{np(1-p)}}\right]\) to calculate the \(Z\) value. Give 2 decimal places.
explanation: The \(\frac{1}{2}\) is a continuity correction. A count of {{x}} is drawn as a bar that starts half a unit below it, at {{x - 0.5}}, so '{{x}} or more' starts from {{x - 0.5}}. For '\(\leq\) Observed' you add \(\frac{1}{2}\) instead. Work out the whole top line before dividing: \(Observed - \frac{1}{2} - np\).
rcode:
n <- {{n}}; p <- 0.5; x <- {{x}}
z <- (x - 0.5 - n * p) / sqrt(n * p * (1 - p))
z
pnorm(z, lower.tail = FALSE)              # approximate Pr[X >= x]
pbinom(x - 1, n, p, lower.tail = FALSE)   # exact binomial, for comparison

prompt: For \(Pr[X \leq Observed]\), how is the \(\frac{1}{2}\) used in the normal approximation?
choices: It is added: \(Observed + \frac{1}{2}\) ;; It is subtracted: \(Observed - \frac{1}{2}\) ;; It is left out, because \(\leq\) already includes the observed value ;; The whole Z value is divided by \(\frac{1}{2}\)
explanation: 'Observed or fewer' includes the whole bar for the observed count, and that bar reaches half a unit above it, so you add \(\frac{1}{2}\). For '\(\geq\) Observed', the bar starts half a unit below, so you subtract. A memory aid: the correction always moves the cut-off outwards, to include the observed count's whole bar.

prompt: In the normal approximation to the binomial, \(\mu = np\) and \(\sigma = \sqrt{np(1-p)}\). Which \(p\) goes into these formulas when you test a hypothesis?
choices: The proportion stated by the null hypothesis ;; The proportion observed in your sample, \(\hat{p}\) ;; The P-value ;; The adjusted proportion \(p'\)
explanation: The test asks how surprising your data would be if the null hypothesis were true, so the expected mean and spread come from the null hypothesis's value of \(p\) (often written \(p_0\)). Your observed proportion \(\hat{p}\) only enters through the observed count.

prompt: Using the excerpt below from a table of upper-tail probabilities for the standard normal distribution, find \(Pr[-{{a}} \lt Z \lt {{b}}]\). Give 4 decimal places.{{z_side(tab_z(c(a, b)), z_curve(c(-a, b)))}}
data:
a <- round(runif(1, 0.5, 2.5), 2); b <- round(runif(1, 0.5, 2.5), 2); ta <- round(pnorm(a, lower.tail = FALSE), 6); tb <- round(pnorm(b, lower.tail = FALSE), 6); key13 <- paste0("Teal: the answer.
Orange: the two tails you subtract. The upper one is the table value for ", b, "; the lower one equals the table value for ", a, " by symmetry.")
explanation: Work with the two tails, because they are what the table gives. By symmetry, \(Pr[Z \lt -{{a}}] = Pr[Z \gt {{a}}]\), so look up {{a}} as a positive number. The area between the two values is the whole distribution (1) minus the lower tail minus the upper tail. A quick sketch of the curve with both tails shaded helps.
worked:
\(Pr[Z \lt -{{a}}] = Pr[Z \gt {{a}}] = {{sprintf('%.6f', ta)}}\)
\(Pr[Z \gt {{b}}] = {{sprintf('%.6f', tb)}}\)
\(1 - {{sprintf('%.6f', ta)}} - {{sprintf('%.6f', tb)}} = {{sprintf('%.4f', 1 - ta - tb)}}\){{z_curve(c(-a, b), c(-a, b), list(c(-Inf, -a), c(b, Inf)), key13, TRUE)}}
rcode:
pnorm({{b}}) - pnorm(-{{a}})   # area between the two values
1 - pnorm({{a}}, lower.tail = FALSE) - pnorm({{b}}, lower.tail = FALSE)   # the same, from the two tails

prompt: True or false: \(Pr[Z \gt {{z}}] = Pr[Z \geq {{z}}]\).
explanation: For a continuous distribution such as the normal, probability is an area under the curve, and a single exact value has no width, so its probability is 0. Including or excluding {{z}} itself makes no difference. Counts are different: for a discrete distribution such as the binomial, \(Pr[X \geq k]\) and \(Pr[X \gt k]\) differ by \(Pr[X = k]\).
rcode: pnorm({{z}}, lower.tail = FALSE)   # the same answer for > and >=

prompt: What does the (2) in \(t_{0.05(2), df}\) mean?
choices: It is a two-tailed test: the 0.05 is split between the two tails, 0.025 in each ;; Square the critical value ;; The test has 2 degrees of freedom ;; Multiply 0.05 by 2
explanation: \(\alpha(2)\) means two-tailed and \(\alpha(1)\) means one-tailed. With \(\alpha(2) = 0.05\), each tail holds 0.025, so it uses the same column as \(\alpha(1) = 0.025\). That is why critical-value tables print the \(\alpha(2)\) and \(\alpha(1)\) rows one above the other. The df after the comma picks the row.

prompt: Using the excerpt below from a table of critical values of the t distribution, find \(t_{ {{a2}}(2), {{df}} }\).{{tab_t(df)}}
explanation: Find the column headed \(\alpha(2) = {{a2}}\) (which is also \(\alpha(1) = {{a2 / 2}}\)), then go down to the row for \(df = {{df}}\). A two-tailed \(\alpha\) is split between the two tails, so {{100 * a2 / 2}}% sits in each. In R, the same value is qt({{1 - a2 / 2}}, {{df}}): {{1 - a2 / 2}}, because {{100 * a2 / 2}}% sits in the upper tail.
rcode: qt({{1 - a2 / 2}}, df = {{df}})   # {{100 * a2 / 2}}% in the upper tail

prompt: Using the excerpt below from a table of critical values of the t distribution, find \(t_{ {{a1}}(1), {{df}} }\), the critical value for a one-tailed test.{{tab_t(df)}}
explanation: \(\alpha(1) = {{a1}}\) puts all of the {{a1}} in one tail, so it is the same column as \(\alpha(2) = {{2 * a1}}\); use the \(\alpha(1)\) heading row. It is smaller than the two-tailed value, \(t_{ {{a1}}(2), {{df}} } = {{sprintf('%.2f', qt(1 - a1 / 2, df))}}\), because the whole {{100 * a1}}% sits in one tail. In R: qt({{1 - a1}}, {{df}}).
rcode: qt({{1 - a1}}, df = {{df}})   # all {{100 * a1}}% in the upper tail

prompt: A sample of \(n = {{n}}\) has \(\bar{Y} = {{ybar}}\) and \(s = {{s}}\). The null hypothesis is \(\mu_0 = {{mu0}}\). Calculate \(SE_{\bar{Y}} = \dfrac{s}{\sqrt{n}}\), then \(t = \dfrac{\bar{Y} - \mu_0}{SE_{\bar{Y}}}\), and the degrees of freedom. Give 2 decimal places.
data: n <- sample(c(9, 16, 25, 36), 1); s <- sample(c(3, 4, 6, 9, 12), 1); se <- s / sqrt(n); mu0 <- sample(seq(20, 60, 5), 1); ybar <- round(mu0 + sample(c(-1, 1), 1) * runif(1, 0.8, 3) * se, 1)
explanation: Subtract on top first, then divide by the standard error, not by \(s\). A negative \(t\) just means \(\bar{Y}\) is below \(\mu_0\). The degrees of freedom for one sample are \(n - 1\).
rcode:
n <- {{n}}; ybar <- {{ybar}}; s <- {{s}}; mu0 <- {{mu0}}
se <- s / sqrt(n)
se
(ybar - mu0) / se
n - 1

prompt: In \(t = \dfrac{\bar{Y} - \mu_0}{SE_{\bar{Y}}}\), what is \(\mu_0\)?
choices: The population mean stated by the null hypothesis ;; The sample mean ;; A mean of zero, always ;; The first observation in the sample
explanation: The subscript 0 is a label for 'null', just as in \(H_0\) and \(p_0\). \(\mu_0\) is the value the null hypothesis says the population mean should be. It is often not zero: for example, a null hypothesis that mean body temperature is 37 degrees C has \(\mu_0 = 37\).

prompt: A 95% confidence interval for \(\mu\) can be written \(\bar{Y} - t_{\alpha(2),df} \cdot SE_{\bar{Y}} \lt \mu \lt \bar{Y} + t_{\alpha(2),df} \cdot SE_{\bar{Y}}\). With \(\bar{Y} = {{ybar}}\), \(SE_{\bar{Y}} = {{se}}\) and \(t_{0.05(2), {{df}} } = {{tc}}\), calculate the lower and upper limits.
data: ybar <- round(runif(1, 10, 50), 1); se <- round(runif(1, 0.5, 3), 2); df <- sample(5:25, 1); tc <- round(qt(0.975, df), 2)
answer_expr: c(ybar - tc * se, ybar + tc * se)
explanation: Read the double inequality as one sentence: '\(\mu\) lies between the lower limit and the upper limit'. In each limit, multiply \(t\) by the standard error first, then subtract it from \(\bar{Y}\) or add it to \(\bar{Y}\). This is the same \(\pm\) idea as \(\bar{Y} \pm 2SE\), with a more exact multiplier.
worked:
\({{tc}} \times {{se}} = {{round(tc * se, 4)}}\)
Lower: \({{ybar}} - {{round(tc * se, 4)}} = {{round(ybar - tc * se, 4)}}\)
Upper: \({{ybar}} + {{round(tc * se, 4)}} = {{round(ybar + tc * se, 4)}}\)
rcode:
{{ybar}} - {{tc}} * {{se}}   # lower limit
{{ybar}} + {{tc}} * {{se}}   # upper limit
qt(0.975, df = {{df}})       # where the critical t comes from

prompt: In a paired t-test, \(t = \dfrac{\bar{d} - \mu_{d0}}{SE_{\bar{d}}}\). What is \(\bar{d}\)?
choices: The mean of the differences, with one difference calculated within each pair ;; The difference between the largest and smallest values in the data ;; An effect size such as Cohen's \(d\) ;; The median of the differences
explanation: In a paired design, you first subtract within each pair to get one difference \(d\) per pair, then treat those differences as a single sample. \(\bar{d}\) is their mean, \(s_d\) is their standard deviation, and \(n\) is the number of pairs. The bar means 'mean of', exactly as in \(\bar{Y}\). The letter \(d\) is reused for Cohen's \(d\), which is something else.

prompt: Hypothetical example. Five lizards are measured before and after a treatment.{{tab}}Using \(d = \text{After} - \text{Before}\) for each lizard, calculate \(\bar{d}\) and the degrees of freedom for a paired t-test.
data:
before <- sample(20:40, 5); d <- sample(-3:8, 5, replace = TRUE); after <- before + d; td <- function(x) paste0('', x, '', collapse = ''); tab <- paste0('', td('Lizard'), td(1:5), '', td('Before'), td(before), '', td('After'), td(after), '
'); dtxt <- paste0(ifelse(d < 0, paste0('(', d, ')'), d), collapse = ' + ')
explanation: Subtract within each pair first, keeping the signs: a decrease gives a negative difference. Then average the differences. The degrees of freedom use the number of pairs, \(n - 1 = 4\), not the total number of measurements (10).
rcode:
before <- c({{lst(before)}})
after  <- c({{lst(after)}})
d <- after - before
d
mean(d)
length(d) - 1
# t.test(after, before, paired = TRUE) runs the whole test

prompt: Two samples have \(n_1 = {{n1}}\), \(s_1 = {{s1}}\) and \(n_2 = {{n2}}\), \(s_2 = {{s2}}\). Calculate the pooled variance \(s_p^2 = \dfrac{df_1 \cdot s_1^2 + df_2 \cdot s_2^2}{df_1 + df_2}\), and then \(SE_{\bar{Y}_1 - \bar{Y}_2} = \sqrt{s_p^2 \left( \dfrac{1}{n_1} + \dfrac{1}{n_2} \right)}\). Give 2 decimal places.
explanation: The values given are standard deviations, so square them first: \(s_1^2 = {{s1^2}}\) and \(s_2^2 = {{s2^2}}\). Each \(df\) is that sample's \(n - 1\). The pooled variance is a weighted average of the two variances, so it always lies between them. For the standard error, add the two fractions inside the bracket first, multiply by \(s_p^2\), and take the square root last.

prompt: What does the subscript in \(SE_{\bar{Y}_1 - \bar{Y}_2}\) tell you?
choices: It is the standard error of the difference between two sample means ;; Subtract the standard error of group 2 from the standard error of group 1 ;; It is the standard error of group 1, minus the mean of group 2 ;; It is two separate standard errors, one per group
explanation: The whole subscript is a name tag for one quantity: the difference \(\bar{Y}_1 - \bar{Y}_2\). The standard error says how much that difference would vary from study to study. It is not found by subtracting two standard errors: uncertainty from both samples adds together, which is why the formula adds \(\frac{1}{n_1} + \frac{1}{n_2}\).

prompt: Find the degrees of freedom for (a) a two-sample t-test with \(n_1 = {{n1}}\) and \(n_2 = {{n2}}\), and (b) a paired t-test on {{np}} pairs.
explanation: For two independent samples, \(df = df_1 + df_2 = (n_1 - 1) + (n_2 - 1) = n_1 + n_2 - 2\). For a paired test, the data become one sample of differences, so \(df = n - 1\), where \(n\) is the number of pairs, not the number of measurements.
rcode:
{{n1}} + {{n2}} - 2   # two-sample
{{np}} - 1            # paired: number of pairs minus 1

prompt: In \(t = \dfrac{(\bar{Y}_1 - \bar{Y}_2) - (\mu_1 - \mu_2)_0}{SE_{\bar{Y}_1 - \bar{Y}_2}}\), what is \((\mu_1 - \mu_2)_0\), and what is it usually?
choices: The difference between population means stated by the null hypothesis; usually 0 ;; The difference between the two sample means; it varies from study to study ;; The first observation in each group ;; The difference in sample sizes; usually 0
explanation: The subscript 0 outside the bracket labels the whole difference as the null hypothesis's value. The usual null hypothesis is 'no difference', so \((\mu_1 - \mu_2)_0 = 0\) and the top of the fraction is just \(\bar{Y}_1 - \bar{Y}_2\). Greek letters are population values; the barred Roman letters are your sample means.

prompt: True or false: you calculate \(t = -{{tv}}\) for a two-tailed test. Because tables of critical t values list only positive numbers, you compare {{tv}} with the critical value.
explanation: The t distribution is symmetrical around 0, so a \(t\) of \(-{{tv}}\) is exactly as extreme as \(+{{tv}}\). For a two-tailed test, compare the absolute value \(|t| = {{tv}}\) with \(t_{\alpha(2),df}\). The sign still tells you the direction of the difference, so keep it when you report \(t\).
rcode: abs(-{{tv}})   # compare this with the critical value

prompt: A two-tailed test gives \(|t| = {{tv}}\) with \(df = {{df}}\). Three of the critical values in that row of the t table are \(t_{0.10(2), {{df}} } = {{c10}}\), \(t_{0.05(2), {{df}} } = {{c05}}\) and \(t_{0.01(2), {{df}} } = {{c01}}\). What can you report about the P-value?
data: df <- sample(5:30, 1); c10 <- round(qt(0.95, df), 3); c05 <- round(qt(0.975, df), 3); c01 <- round(qt(0.995, df), 3); labs <- c('\\(P \\gt 0.10\\)', '\\(0.05 \\lt P \\lt 0.10\\)', '\\(0.01 \\lt P \\lt 0.05\\)', '\\(P \\lt 0.01\\)'); idx <- sample(2:4, 1); lo <- c(0, c10, c05, c01)[idx]; hi <- c(c10, c05, c01, c01 + 1.5)[idx]; tv <- round(runif(1, lo + 0.03, hi - 0.03), 2); ok <- labs[idx]; w <- labs[-idx]; where <- c('', paste('larger than', c10, 'but smaller than', c05), paste('larger than', c05, 'but smaller than', c01), paste('larger than', c01))[idx]
explanation: Compare \(|t|\) with the critical values in its row. They get larger as \(\alpha\) gets smaller, and each one that \(|t|\) passes means \(P\) is below that \(\alpha\). Here {{tv}} is {{where}}, so {{ok}}. When the exact \(df\) is not listed in a table, a safe choice is the next lower \(df\) that is; its critical value is slightly larger, so the test is slightly cautious.
rcode: 2 * pt({{tv}}, df = {{df}}, lower.tail = FALSE)   # the exact two-tailed P-value

prompt: R gives the area in the upper tail beyond \(t = {{tv}}\) with \(df = {{df}}\): pt({{tv}}, df = {{df}}, lower.tail = FALSE) returns {{sprintf('%.4f', a)}}. What is the P-value for a two-tailed test? Give 4 decimal places.
data: tv <- round(runif(1, 1.2, 3), 2); df <- sample(8:30, 1); a <- round(pt(tv, df, lower.tail = FALSE), 4)
explanation: pt() with lower.tail = FALSE gives the area in one tail only. A two-tailed test (for example \(H_A: \mu \neq \mu_0\)) counts results that are equally extreme in either direction, and the t distribution is symmetrical, so the other tail has the same area: double it. This matches the \(\alpha(2)\) heading of the t table. t.test() reports the two-tailed P-value directly.
rcode: 2 * pt({{tv}}, df = {{df}}, lower.tail = FALSE)   # both tails

prompt: A 95% confidence interval for a variance is \(\dfrac{df}{\chi^2_{\frac{\alpha}{2}, df}} \cdot s^2 \lt \sigma^2 \lt \dfrac{df}{\chi^2_{1-\frac{\alpha}{2}, df}} \cdot s^2\), with \(\alpha = 0.05\). What does the subscript \(\frac{\alpha}{2}\) tell you to do?
choices: Look up the \(\chi^2\) value with 0.025 of the distribution in the upper tail ;; Divide the \(\chi^2\) value by 2 ;; Look up the \(\chi^2\) value for \(df = 2\) ;; Use \(\alpha = 0.05\), then halve the width of the interval
explanation: Only \(\alpha\) is divided. The interval needs a limit on each side, so the 0.05 is split between the two tails, 0.025 in each. With a table of upper-tail areas, \(\chi^2_{0.025, df}\) is the large value (2.5% of the distribution above it) and \(\chi^2_{0.975, df}\) is the small value (97.5% above it). Dividing by the large value gives the lower limit. A \(\chi^2\) goodness-of-fit or contingency test uses \(\alpha\) without halving, because it uses only the upper tail. R's qchisq() works with the lower tail unless told otherwise, so always check which tail a table or function reports.
rcode:
qchisq(0.025, df = 7, lower.tail = FALSE)   # large value: 2.5% above it
qchisq(0.975, df = 7, lower.tail = FALSE)   # small value: 97.5% above it

prompt: A sample of \(n = {{n}}\) has variance \(s^2 = {{s2}}\), so \(df = n - 1 = {{df}}\). From a table of upper-tail areas, \(\chi^2_{0.025, {{df}} } = {{hi}}\) and \(\chi^2_{0.975, {{df}} } = {{lo}}\). Calculate the 95% confidence interval \(\dfrac{df}{\chi^2_{\frac{\alpha}{2}, df}} \cdot s^2 \lt \sigma^2 \lt \dfrac{df}{\chi^2_{1-\frac{\alpha}{2}, df}} \cdot s^2\). Give 3 decimal places.
data: n <- sample(6:11, 1); df <- n - 1; s2 <- round(runif(1, 0.5, 10), 2); hi <- round(qchisq(0.975, df), 2); lo <- round(qchisq(0.025, df), 2)
answer_expr: c(df * s2 / hi, df * s2 / lo)
explanation: \(df \cdot s^2\) is the same for both limits; only the \(\chi^2\) value changes. Dividing by the larger \(\chi^2\) ({{hi}}) gives the smaller number, so it is the lower limit. The interval is not symmetrical around \(s^2\), because the \(\chi^2\) distribution is skewed. Taking the square root of both limits gives a confidence interval for \(\sigma\).
worked:
\(df \cdot s^2 = {{df}} \times {{s2}} = {{df * s2}}\)
Lower: \(\dfrac{ {{df * s2}} }{ {{hi}} } = {{round(df * s2 / hi, 4)}}\)
Upper: \(\dfrac{ {{df * s2}} }{ {{lo}} } = {{round(df * s2 / lo, 4)}}\)
rcode:
n <- {{n}}; s2 <- {{s2}}; df <- n - 1
df * s2 / qchisq(0.025, df, lower.tail = FALSE)   # lower limit
df * s2 / qchisq(0.975, df, lower.tail = FALSE)   # upper limit

prompt: After a log transformation, data are often written \(Y' = \ln(Y)\). What does the prime mark in \(Y'\) mean?
choices: A transformed version of \(Y\) ;; The derivative of \(Y\) ;; \(Y\) squared ;; The predicted value of \(Y\)
explanation: A prime marks 'a modified version of'. The same mark appears in \(p' = \frac{X+2}{n+4}\), an adjusted proportion, and in \(p' = \arcsin[\sqrt{p}]\), a transformed proportion: three different modifications share one symbol. A predicted value uses a hat instead, as in \(\hat{Y}\).

prompt: Count data include zeros, so they are transformed with \(Y' = \ln(Y + 1)\). Transform the value \(Y = {{y}}\). Give 3 decimal places.
explanation: Inside the brackets first: add 1, then take the natural log. \(\ln(0)\) does not exist, which is why 1 is added; \(\ln(0 + 1) = \ln(1) = 0\). The 1 is added to every value, not only the zeros. Use the ln key, not the log key, which is base 10.
rcode:
log({{y}} + 1)   # in R, log() is the natural log, ln
log1p({{y}})     # a built-in shortcut for log(1 + y)

prompt: Data were analysed after the transformation \(Y' = \ln(Y)\), and the mean of the transformed data is \(\bar{Y}' = {{m}}\). Back-transform this mean to the original scale. Give 2 decimal places.
explanation: To undo \(\ln\), raise \(e\) to that power: \(e^{\bar{Y}'}\). The result is on the original scale, but it is not the same as the ordinary mean of the original data: averaging logs and then back-transforming gives a different kind of average. Confidence limits are back-transformed the same way, one limit at a time.
rcode: exp({{m}})   # exp() undoes log()

prompt: Counts are transformed with \(Y' = \sqrt{Y + \frac{1}{2}}\). Transform the two values \(Y = {{y[1]}}\) and \(Y = {{y[2]}}\). Give 2 decimal places.
explanation: The square-root sign covers \(Y + \frac{1}{2}\), so add the half first, then take the root. Taking \(\sqrt{Y}\) first and then adding \(\frac{1}{2}\) gives a different number: for \(Y = {{y[1]}}\), that would be {{round(sqrt(y[1]) + 0.5, 2)}} instead of {{round(sqrt(y[1] + 0.5), 2)}}.

prompt: Which formula means 'add 1 to each value, then take the natural logarithm'?
explanation: Whatever sits inside the brackets after \(\ln\) is done first. In \(\ln(Y + 1)\) the 1 is inside, so it is added before the log is taken. In \(\ln(Y) + 1\), the log is taken first and 1 is added afterwards. For \(Y = 9\), these give 2.303 and 3.197.
rcode:
log(9 + 1)   # ln(Y + 1)
log(9) + 1   # ln(Y) + 1: a different number

prompt: Rank these six values from smallest to largest: \({{lst(shown)}}\). Two of the values are tied. What rank does each of the tied values get?
data: v <- sort(sample(10:60, 5)); pos <- sample(1:4, 1); x <- sort(c(v, v[pos])); shown <- sample(x)
explanation: Tied values share the average of the ranks they would have taken. Here the two values of {{v[pos]}} occupy ranks {{pos}} and {{pos + 1}}, so each gets \(\frac{ {{pos}} + {{pos + 1}} }{2} = {{pos + 0.5}}\). The next value gets rank {{pos + 2}}: the tie uses up both ranks.
rcode:
x <- c({{lst(shown)}})
rank(x)   # tied values get the average of their ranks

prompt: Group 1 is \(\lbrace {{lst(g1)}} \rbrace\) and group 2 is \(\lbrace {{lst(g2)}} \rbrace\). Rank all seven values together, from smallest to largest, then calculate the rank sum for group 1, \(R_1\).
data: allv <- sample(5:60, 7); g1 <- allv[1:3]; g2 <- allv[4:7]; r <- rank(allv); R1 <- sum(r[1:3])
explanation: Rank both groups together, as one list, then add up the ranks that belong to group 1. Ranking each group separately is a common slip. A useful check: the ranks of all \(N\) values add to \(\frac{N(N+1)}{2}\), here \(\frac{7 \times 8}{2} = 28\), so \(R_1 + R_2 = 28\).
rcode:
g1 <- c({{lst(g1)}}); g2 <- c({{lst(g2)}})
r <- rank(c(g1, g2))   # rank everything together
r
sum(r[1:3])            # the ranks that belong to group 1

prompt: For a Mann-Whitney U test, \(n_1 = {{n1}}\), \(n_2 = {{n2}}\), and the rank sum for group 1 is \(R_1 = {{R1}}\). Calculate \(U_1 = n_1 n_2 + \dfrac{n_1(n_1 + 1)}{2} - R_1\), then \(U_2 = n_1 n_2 - U_1\), and the test statistic \(U = \max(U_1, U_2)\).
explanation: \(n_1 n_2\) means \(n_1 \times n_2\), and \(n_1(n_1 + 1)\) means \(n_1 \times (n_1 + 1)\): work out the bracket first, then divide by 2. Add the first two terms, then subtract \(R_1\). \(\max\) means 'the larger of'. A check: \(U_1 + U_2\) always equals \(n_1 n_2\), and neither can be negative.

prompt: What does \(U = \max(U_1, U_2)\) mean?
choices: \(U\) is whichever of \(U_1\) and \(U_2\) is larger ;; \(U = U_1 + U_2\) ;; \(U\) is the average of \(U_1\) and \(U_2\) ;; \(U = U_1 \times U_2\)
explanation: \(\max(\ )\) picks the largest of the values listed in the brackets, and \(\min(\ )\) picks the smallest. The commas only separate the values; nothing is added or multiplied. The test compares this larger \(U\) with a critical value: if \(U\) is greater than or equal to the critical value, \(P \leq \alpha\).
rcode: max(7, 5)   # the larger value

prompt: Using the excerpt below from a table of critical values for the Mann-Whitney U test, find \(U_{ {{a}}(2), {{n1}}, {{n2}} }\) for \(n_1 = {{n1}}\) and \(n_2 = {{n2}}\).{{tab_u(n1, n2)}}
data: a <- sample(c(0.05, 0.05, 0.01), 1); repeat { n1 <- sample(4:15, 1); n2 <- sample(4:15, 1); cands <- 0:(n1 * n2); ok <- cands[pwilcox(cands - 1, n1, n2, lower.tail = FALSE) <= a / 2]; if (length(ok) > 0) break }; ucrit <- min(ok)
explanation: The subscript lists what you need: the significance level and number of tails, \({{a}}(2)\), then the two sample sizes. First pick the panel for \(\alpha(2) = {{a}}\), then find where \(n_1\) and \(n_2\) meet. The table is symmetrical, so it does not matter which sample you call \(n_1\). Unlike a t or Z table, there are no degrees of freedom: you look up the sample sizes directly. If your \(U\) is greater than or equal to this critical value, \(P \leq {{a}}\).
rcode:
n1 <- {{n1}}; n2 <- {{n2}}
U <- 0:(n1 * n2)
# the smallest U with at most {{100 * a / 2}}% of the null distribution at or above it
min(U[pwilcox(U - 1, n1, n2, lower.tail = FALSE) <= {{a / 2}}])

prompt: A sign test on paired data finds {{np}} positive and {{nn}} negative differences (differences of zero are dropped). Under the null hypothesis, the number of positive differences follows a binomial distribution. Which values does it use?
data: np <- sample(3:12, 1); nn <- sample(setdiff(1:8, np), 1); n <- np + nn
explanation: The null hypothesis says a difference is equally likely to be positive or negative, so \(p = 0.5\). \(n\) counts every non-zero difference, here \({{np}} + {{nn}} = {{n}}\). Do not confuse \(p = 0.5\) with the significance level \(\alpha = 0.05\). The observed proportion \(\frac{ {{np}} }{ {{n}} }\) is \(\hat{p}\), not \(p\).
rcode: binom.test({{np}}, {{n}}, p = 0.5)   # the sign test is a binomial test

prompt: Proportions are sometimes transformed with \(p' = \arcsin[\sqrt{p}]\). In what order are the steps done?
choices: Take the square root of \(p\), then take the arcsine of the result ;; Take the arcsine of \(p\), then take the square root ;; Multiply \(\arcsin\) by \(\sqrt{p}\) ;; Take the square root of both 'arcsin' and \(p\) separately
explanation: Read from the inside out: \(\sqrt{p}\) sits inside the square brackets, so it is done first, and \(\arcsin\) is then applied to that result. \(\arcsin\) is the name of a function (the inverse sine), like \(\ln\), so it is not multiplied by anything. If the data are percentages, convert them to proportions first.

prompt: For two groups with \(n_1 = {{n1}}\) and \(n_2 = {{n2}}\), you calculate \(U_1 = {{u1}}\) and \(U_2 = {{u2}}\). R's wilcox.test() reports W = {{u1}}. How does R's W relate to U?
choices: W is the same statistic as U; R reports one of the two U values, depending on which group is listed first ;; W is a different statistic, so it cannot be compared with U ;; W is the rank sum \(R_1\) ;; W is \(U\) divided by \(n_1 n_2\)
data: n1 <- sample(5:10, 1); n2 <- sample(5:10, 1); u1 <- sample(ceiling(n1 * n2 * 0.15):floor(n1 * n2 * 0.45), 1); u2 <- n1 * n2 - u1
explanation: W and U are the same statistic under different letters; W comes from Wilcoxon's version of the test. The two U values always add up to \(n_1 n_2 = {{n1 * n2}}\), and R reports one of them depending on the order of the groups. By hand, use the larger one, \(U = \max(U_1, U_2) = {{u2}}\), with the table. In R, read the P-value, which is the same whichever group comes first.
rcode:
# with the two groups of data in x and y:
wilcox.test(x, y)   # W is one of the two U values
wilcox.test(y, x)   # W is the other one; the P-value is the same

prompt: Two samples, \(n_1 = {{n1}}\) and \(n_2 = {{n2}}\), are too large for the table of critical U values, and \(U = {{U}}\). Convert U to a Z statistic with \(Z = \dfrac{2U - n_1 n_2}{\sqrt{\dfrac{n_1 n_2 (n_1 + n_2 + 1)}{3}}}\). Give 3 decimal places.
data: n1 <- sample(16:30, 1); n2 <- sample(16:30, 1); U <- sample(ceiling(n1 * n2 * 0.55):floor(n1 * n2 * 0.85), 1)
explanation: Work the top and bottom separately. On top, \(2U\) means \(2 \times U\): double it, then subtract \(n_1 n_2\). Underneath, multiply \(n_1\), \(n_2\) and the bracket \((n_1 + n_2 + 1)\), divide by 3, and take the square root of the whole thing last. Then compare \(Z\) with the standard normal distribution (1.96 for \(\alpha = 0.05\), two-tailed). The approximation is reliable when both samples are larger than about 10; for smaller samples, use the U table.
rcode:
n1 <- {{n1}}; n2 <- {{n2}}; U <- {{U}}
Z <- (2 * U - n1 * n2) / sqrt(n1 * n2 * (n1 + n2 + 1) / 3)
Z
2 * pnorm(Z, lower.tail = FALSE)   # approximate two-tailed P-value

prompt: With \(\alpha = 0.05\), find the probability of making at least one Type I error across \(N = {{N}}\) independent tests, using \(Pr[\text{at least one Type I error}] = 1 - (1 - \alpha)^N\). Give 3 decimal places.
explanation: Brackets first: \(1 - \alpha = 0.95\) is the chance of no error in one test. The exponent \(N\) applies to the whole bracket, so \(0.95^{ {{N}} }\) is the chance of no errors in all {{N}} tests. Subtracting that from 1 gives the complement: at least one error. This rising error rate is why many separate t-tests are replaced by one ANOVA.

prompt: In ANOVA, \(df_{error} = N - k\). What are \(N\) and \(k\)?
choices: \(N\) is the total number of observations in all groups, and \(k\) is the number of groups ;; \(N\) is the number of observations in each group, and \(k\) is the number of groups ;; \(N\) is the number of groups, and \(k\) is the total number of observations ;; \(N\) is the number of tests, and \(k\) is the number of categories
explanation: Capital \(N\) is the grand total sample size, and \(n_i\) (lower case, with a subscript) is the size of group \(i\), so \(N = \sum n_i\). \(k\) counts the groups. The same letters are reused elsewhere: \(N\) is the number of tests in \(1 - (1 - \alpha)^N\), and \(k\) is the number of categories in a \(\chi^2\) test. Read each letter in its own formula.

prompt: An ANOVA compares \(k = {{k}}\) groups with sample sizes \(n_i = {{lst(ni)}}\). Calculate \(df_{groups} = k - 1\) and \(df_{error} = N - k\).
data: k <- sample(3:5, 1); ni <- sample(4:10, k, replace = TRUE)
explanation: First add the group sizes to get \(N = {{sum(ni)}}\). Then \(df_{groups} = {{k}} - 1\) and \(df_{error} = {{sum(ni)}} - {{k}}\). The two add up to \(N - 1\), the total degrees of freedom.
rcode:
ni <- c({{lst(ni)}})
k <- length(ni)
k - 1         # df groups
sum(ni) - k   # df error

prompt: Three groups have sizes \(n_i = {{lst(ni)}}\) and means \(\bar{Y}_i = {{lst(mi)}}\). Calculate the grand mean \(\bar{Y} = \dfrac{\sum (n_i \bar{Y}_i)}{N}\). Give 2 decimal places.
explanation: Inside the brackets, multiply each group's mean by its own size, then add the three products. Divide by \(N\), the total number of observations. This gives larger groups more weight. Simply averaging the three means gives {{round(mean(mi), 2)}}, which is only correct when the groups are the same size.
worked: \(\bar{Y} = \dfrac{ {{paste0(ni, ' \\times ', mi, collapse = ' + ')}} }{ {{paste(ni, collapse = ' + ')}} } = \dfrac{ {{sum(ni * mi)}} }{ {{sum(ni)}} } = {{round(sum(ni * mi) / sum(ni), 4)}}\)
rcode:
ni <- c({{lst(ni)}}); mi <- c({{lst(mi)}})
sum(ni * mi) / sum(ni)   # weighted by group size
mean(mi)                 # unweighted: right only for equal group sizes

prompt: Three groups each have \(n_i = {{n}}\) observations, with means \(\bar{Y}_i = {{lst(mi)}}\), so the grand mean is \(\bar{Y} = {{gm}}\). Calculate \(SS_{groups} = \sum_{i=1}^{k} n_i (\bar{Y}_i - \bar{Y})^2\).
data: n <- sample(4:8, 1); mi <- nice_sample(3, 8, 20); gm <- mean(mi)
explanation: The sum runs from \(i = 1\) to \(k = 3\): one term per group. In each term, subtract first (the bracket), then square, then multiply by \(n_i\). The square sits outside the bracket but inside the sum, so it applies to each group's difference separately.
worked:
\(SS_{groups} = {{paste0(n, '(', mi, ' - ', gm, ')^2', collapse = ' + ')}}\)
\(= {{paste0(n, ' \\times ', (mi - gm)^2, collapse = ' + ')}} = {{n * sum((mi - gm)^2)}}\)
rcode:
n <- {{n}}; mi <- c({{lst(mi)}})
Ybar <- mean(mi)
sum(n * (mi - Ybar)^2)

prompt: Three groups have sizes \(n_i = {{lst(ni)}}\) and standard deviations \(s_i = {{lst(si)}}\). Calculate \(SS_{error} = \sum_{i=1}^{k} s_i^2 (n_i - 1)\). Give 2 decimal places.
explanation: Check what you are given: standard deviations, so square each one first to get the variance \(s_i^2\). Then multiply by that group's \(n_i - 1\), and add the three terms. Each term is the sum of squares within one group, so \(SS_{error}\) collects the spread inside all of the groups.
rcode:
ni <- c({{lst(ni)}}); si <- c({{lst(si)}})
sum(si^2 * (ni - 1))

prompt: An ANOVA with \(k = {{k}}\) groups and \(N = {{N}}\) observations has \(SS_{groups} = {{ssg}}\) and \(SS_{error} = {{sse}}\). Calculate \(MS_{groups} = \dfrac{SS_{groups}}{df_{groups}}\), \(MS_{error} = \dfrac{SS_{error}}{df_{error}}\), and \(F = \dfrac{MS_{groups}}{MS_{error}}\). Give 2 decimal places.
data: k <- sample(3:5, 1); N <- k * sample(5:8, 1); ssg <- round(runif(1, 20, 120), 1); sse <- round(runif(1, 40, 200), 1)
explanation: Each mean square is a sum of squares divided by its own degrees of freedom: \(df_{groups} = k - 1 = {{k - 1}}\) and \(df_{error} = N - k = {{N - k}}\). \(F\) divides the two mean squares, not the two sums of squares. If the null hypothesis is true, both mean squares estimate the same variance, so \(F\) is close to 1.
rcode:
k <- {{k}}; N <- {{N}}; SSg <- {{ssg}}; SSe <- {{sse}}
MSg <- SSg / (k - 1)
MSe <- SSe / (N - k)
MSg; MSe
MSg / MSe                                   # F
pf(MSg / MSe, k - 1, N - k, lower.tail = FALSE)   # its P-value

prompt: An ANOVA has \(SS_{groups} = {{ssg}}\) and \(SS_{error} = {{sse}}\). Using \(SS_{total} = SS_{groups} + SS_{error}\), calculate \(R^2 = \dfrac{SS_{groups}}{SS_{total}}\). Give 3 decimal places.
explanation: \(SS_{total}\) is not given, so build it first by adding the two parts. \(R^2\) is then the share of all the variation that is explained by differences between the groups. It is a proportion, so it must lie between 0 and 1. Dividing \(SS_{groups}\) by \(SS_{error}\) instead is a common slip.
rcode:
SSg <- {{ssg}}; SSe <- {{sse}}
SSg / (SSg + SSe)

prompt: After an ANOVA with \(k = {{k}}\) groups, how many unplanned pairwise comparisons are possible? Use \(\dbinom{k}{2} = \dfrac{k!}{2!(k-2)!}\).
explanation: '\(k\) choose 2' counts the different pairs you can make from \(k\) groups. Most of the factorial cancels: \(\dfrac{k!}{2!(k-2)!} = \dfrac{k(k-1)}{2}\). The number of comparisons grows quickly as groups are added, and so does the chance of at least one Type I error. Group 2 versus group 3 is the same comparison as group 3 versus group 2 (only the sign of the difference changes), so each pair is counted once.
rcode: choose({{k}}, 2)

prompt: In \(F_{0.05(1), {{d1}}, {{d2}} }\), which number is the numerator (groups) degrees of freedom?
explanation: The subscript reads in a fixed order: the significance level and number of tails, \(0.05(1)\); then \(df_1\), the numerator (groups); then \(df_2\), the denominator (error). The (1) means one-tailed: F tests use only the upper tail, because real differences between means can only make F larger. In an F table, \(df_1\) picks the column and \(df_2\) picks the row.
rcode: qf(0.95, df1 = {{d1}}, df2 = {{d2}})   # numerator df first, then denominator df

prompt: Using the excerpt below from a table of critical values of the F distribution, find \(F_{0.05(1), {{d1}}, {{d2}} }\).{{tab_f(d1, d2)}}
explanation: The numerator df ({{d1}}) picks the column and the denominator df ({{d2}}) picks the row; swapping them gives a different value. If your calculated F is greater than or equal to this critical value, \(P \leq 0.05\). In R: qf(0.95, {{d1}}, {{d2}}).

prompt: Two group means are \(\bar{Y}_i = {{yi}}\) (\(n_i = {{ni}}\)) and \(\bar{Y}_j = {{yj}}\) (\(n_j = {{nj}}\)), and \(MS_{error} = {{msE}}\). Calculate \(SE = \sqrt{MS_{error}\left(\dfrac{1}{n_i} + \dfrac{1}{n_j}\right)}\), then \(q = \dfrac{\bar{Y}_i - \bar{Y}_j}{SE}\). Give 3 decimal places for SE and 2 for \(q\).
data: msE <- round(runif(1, 1, 6), 2); ni <- sample(4:10, 1); nj <- sample(4:10, 1); se <- sqrt(msE * (1 / ni + 1 / nj)); d <- round(runif(1, 1, 4) * se, 2); yj <- sample(15:30, 1); yi <- yj + d
explanation: Work from the inside out: add the two fractions, multiply by \(MS_{error}\), then take the square root of the whole thing. The subscripts \(i\) and \(j\) just name the two groups being compared. \(MS_{error}\) comes from the whole ANOVA, so every pair of groups uses the same one.
rcode:
MSe <- {{msE}}; ni <- {{ni}}; nj <- {{nj}}
SE <- sqrt(MSe * (1 / ni + 1 / nj))
SE
({{yi}} - {{yj}}) / SE

prompt: Using the excerpt below from a table of critical values of the Tukey-Kramer \(q\) distribution, find \(q_{0.05, {{k}}, {{df}} }\) for \(k = {{k}}\) groups and \(df = N - k = {{df}}\).{{tab_q(k, df)}}
explanation: The subscript tells you where to look: the significance level, then \(k\) (the number of groups, which picks the column), then \(df = N - k\) (the error degrees of freedom, which picks the row). Use \(k\) for the whole ANOVA, even though you are comparing only two groups at a time.
rcode:
qtukey(0.95, nmeans = {{k}}, df = {{df}}) / sqrt(2)
# R's q is larger by a factor of sqrt(2) than the q in these formulas

prompt: True or false: because \(SS_{total} = SS_{groups} + SS_{error}\), it is also true that \(MS_{total} = MS_{groups} + MS_{error}\).
explanation: Sums of squares add up, and so do their degrees of freedom: \(df_{total} = df_{groups} + df_{error}\). But each mean square is a sum of squares divided by a different df, so the mean squares do not add up. That is why an ANOVA table gives SS and df for the total row, but usually leaves its MS blank.

prompt: Using the excerpt below from a table of critical values of the F distribution, find \(F_{0.05(1), {{d1}}, {{d2}} }\), and then \(F_{0.05(1), {{d2}}, {{d1}} }\), with the two degrees of freedom swapped.{{tab_f(c(d1, d2), c(d2, d1))}}
explanation: Unlike the table for the Mann-Whitney U test, the F table is not symmetrical. The first number after \(0.05(1)\) is always the numerator (groups) df, which picks the column, and the second is the denominator (error) df, which picks the row. Swapping them gives a very different critical value, so check which df belongs where before looking anything up.
worked:
Column {{d1}}, row {{d2}}: {{round(qf(0.95, d1, d2), 2)}}
Column {{d2}}, row {{d1}}: {{round(qf(0.95, d2, d1), 2)}}
rcode:
qf(0.95, df1 = {{d1}}, df2 = {{d2}})
qf(0.95, df1 = {{d2}}, df2 = {{d1}})   # swapped: a different value

prompt: An ANOVA compares just two groups: \(n_1 = {{n1}}\), \(s_1 = {{s1}}\) and \(n_2 = {{n2}}\), \(s_2 = {{s2}}\). Calculate \(MS_{error} = \dfrac{SS_{error}}{df_{error}}\), with \(SS_{error} = \sum s_i^2 (n_i - 1)\) and \(df_{error} = N - k\). Then calculate the pooled variance from the two-sample t-test, \(s_p^2 = \dfrac{df_1 s_1^2 + df_2 s_2^2}{df_1 + df_2}\). Give 2 decimal places.
explanation: The two are the same calculation. \(SS_{error}\) is the top of the pooled variance, and \(df_{error} = N - k = n_1 + n_2 - 2 = df_1 + df_2\) is its bottom. So the error mean square is the pooled variance, extended from two groups to any number of groups. With exactly two groups, the ANOVA \(F\) equals the square of the two-sample \(t\), and the two tests give the same P-value. Like the pooled variance, \(MS_{error}\) assumes the groups have similar variances.
rcode:
n <- c({{n1}}, {{n2}}); s <- c({{s1}}, {{s2}})
sum(s^2 * (n - 1)) / (sum(n) - 2)   # MS error = pooled variance

prompt: An ANOVA on four groups rejects \(H_0: \mu_1 = \mu_2 = \mu_3 = \mu_4\) in favour of \(H_A\): at least one \(\mu_i\) is different from the others. What does this tell you?
choices: The means are not all equal; a separate step, such as Tukey-Kramer comparisons, is needed to find which ones differ ;; Exactly one mean differs from the other three ;; All four means differ from each other ;; \(\mu_1\) differs from \(\mu_2\)
explanation: 'At least one' includes one, two or more. The null hypothesis says all the means are equal, so rejecting it says only that they are not all equal; it does not say how many differ, or which ones. That is why a significant ANOVA is followed by unplanned (post hoc) comparisons.

prompt: Hypothetical example. After an ANOVA and Tukey-Kramer comparisons, the group means are plotted with letters above them: {{s$letters}}.{{s$svg}}Which pairs of groups differ significantly?
explanation: Two groups differ significantly only when they share no letter. Here the pairs with no letter in common are {{s$dif}}; the pairs that share a letter ({{s$same}}) are not significantly different. {{s$note}} The letters come from the Tukey-Kramer tests, not from the error bars, so do not judge significance by whether the bars overlap.

prompt: \(S_{XY} = \sum (X_i - \bar{X})(Y_i - \bar{Y})\) is called the sum of products. What does it tell you to do?
choices: For each individual, multiply its X deviation by its Y deviation, then add up the products ;; Add up all the X deviations and all the Y deviations, then multiply the two totals ;; Multiply \(\bar{X}\) by \(\bar{Y}\) ;; Square the X deviations and the Y deviations, then add them
explanation: Two brackets side by side are multiplied, and both sit inside the \(\sum\), so the multiplying happens for each individual \(i\) before anything is added. Multiplying the two totals would always give 0, because deviations from a mean add to zero. The subscript \(i\) pairs each \(X\) with the \(Y\) from the same individual. The order of the rows does not matter, and the values are not ranked, as long as each \(X\) stays with the \(Y\) from the same individual.

prompt: Your data are \(X = \lbrace {{lst(X)}} \rbrace\), so \(n = 4\) and \(\bar{X} = {{mean(X)}}\). Calculate \(SS_X\) both ways: \(\sum (X_i - \bar{X})^2\), and \(\sum (X_i^2) - \dfrac{(\sum X_i)^2}{n}\).
explanation: The two forms always give the same answer, so they are a useful check on each other. In the second form, \(\sum (X_i^2)\) squares each value and then adds, while \((\sum X_i)^2\) adds first and then squares the total once. Divide \((\sum X_i)^2\) by \(n\) before subtracting.
rcode:
X <- c({{lst(X)}})
sum((X - mean(X))^2)               # deviation form
sum(X^2) - sum(X)^2 / length(X)    # computational form: same answer

prompt: For \(n = 5\) pairs of values, \(\sum X_i = {{sum(X)}}\), \(\sum Y_i = {{sum(Y)}}\), and \(\sum (X_i Y_i) = {{sum(X * Y)}}\). Calculate \(S_{XY} = \sum (X_i Y_i) - \dfrac{(\sum X_i)(\sum Y_i)}{n}\). Give 2 decimal places.
explanation: \(\sum (X_i Y_i)\) multiplies within each pair, then adds. \((\sum X_i)(\sum Y_i)\) adds each variable first, then multiplies the two totals. They are different numbers. Divide the product of the totals by \(n\), then subtract. \(S_{XY}\) can be negative; a negative value goes with a negative relationship.
worked: \(S_{XY} = {{sum(X * Y)}} - \dfrac{ {{sum(X)}} \times {{sum(Y)}} }{5} = {{sum(X * Y)}} - {{sum(X) * sum(Y) / 5}} = {{sum(X * Y) - sum(X) * sum(Y) / 5}}\)
rcode:
sumX <- {{sum(X)}}; sumY <- {{sum(Y)}}; sumXY <- {{sum(X * Y)}}; n <- 5
sumXY - sumX * sumY / n

prompt: From a sample, \(S_{XY} = {{sxy}}\), \(SS_X = {{ssx}}\) and \(SS_Y = {{ssy}}\). Calculate the correlation coefficient \(r = \dfrac{S_{XY}}{\sqrt{SS_X \cdot SS_Y}}\). Give 3 decimal places.
data: X <- sample(1:12, 6); Y <- round(2 + sample(c(-1, 1), 1) * 0.8 * X + rnorm(6, 0, 2)); sxy <- round(sum((X - mean(X)) * (Y - mean(Y))), 2); ssx <- round(sum((X - mean(X))^2), 2); ssy <- round(sum((Y - mean(Y))^2), 2)
explanation: The square root covers the whole denominator: multiply \(SS_X\) by \(SS_Y\) first, then take the root. Taking \(\sqrt{SS_X}\) and then multiplying by \(SS_Y\) is a common slip. \(r\) must fall between \(-1\) and \(+1\); an answer outside that range means the root went on the wrong part.

prompt: A sample of \(n = {{n}}\) gives \(r = {{r}}\). Calculate \(SE_r = \sqrt{\dfrac{1 - r^2}{n - 2}}\), then \(t = \dfrac{r}{SE_r}\), and \(df = n - 2\). Give 3 decimal places for \(SE_r\) and 2 for \(t\).
explanation: In \(1 - r^2\), the square applies only to \(r\): square first, then subtract from 1. Then divide by \(n - 2\), and take the square root of the whole fraction last. The degrees of freedom for a correlation are \(n - 2\), not \(n - 1\).

prompt: Which pairing of sample estimate and population parameter is correct?
choices: \(r\) estimates \(\rho\), and \(b\) estimates \(\beta\) ;; \(\rho\) estimates \(r\), and \(\beta\) estimates \(b\) ;; \(r\) estimates \(\beta\), and \(b\) estimates \(\rho\) ;; \(r^2\) estimates \(\rho\), and \(a\) estimates \(\beta\)
explanation: This is the same convention as \(\bar{Y}\) and \(\mu\), or \(s\) and \(\sigma\): Roman letters are calculated from your sample, and Greek letters are the unknown population values. \(\rho\) (rho) is the population correlation and \(\beta\) (beta) is the population slope. Careful: \(\beta\) is also used for the Type II error rate, which is unrelated.

prompt: Calculate Fisher's \(z\) transformation of \(r = {{r}}\): \(z = 0.5 \ln\left(\dfrac{1 + r}{1 - r}\right)\). Give 3 decimal places.
explanation: Inside the brackets first: work out the fraction, then take the natural log (the ln key, not log), and multiply by 0.5 last. This lower-case \(z\) is not the standard normal \(Z\): it is a stretched version of \(r\) whose sampling distribution is closer to normal, which makes a confidence interval possible.

prompt: Fisher's \(z = {{z}}\) from a sample of \(n = {{n}}\). Calculate \(\sigma_z = \sqrt{\dfrac{1}{n - 3}}\), then the 95% confidence interval for \(\zeta\): \(z \pm 1.96\,\sigma_z\). Give 3 decimal places.
explanation: \(\zeta\) (zeta) is the Greek, population version of \(z\), following the usual rule for Greek letters. Multiply 1.96 by \(\sigma_z\) first, then subtract and add. These limits are still on the \(z\) scale; they are back-transformed to give limits for \(\rho\).
worked:
\(\sigma_z = \sqrt{\dfrac{1}{ {{n}} - 3}} = \sqrt{ {{round(1 / (n - 3), 6)}} } = {{round(sz, 4)}}\)
\(1.96 \times {{round(sz, 4)}} = {{round(1.96 * sz, 4)}}\)
Limits: \({{z}} \pm {{round(1.96 * sz, 4)}}\), giving \({{round(z - 1.96 * sz, 4)}}\) and \({{round(z + 1.96 * sz, 4)}}\)
rcode:
z <- {{z}}; n <- {{n}}
sigma_z <- sqrt(1 / (n - 3))
sigma_z
z - 1.96 * sigma_z   # lower limit
z + 1.96 * sigma_z   # upper limit

prompt: Back-transform Fisher's \(z = {{z}}\) to a correlation using \(r = \dfrac{e^{2z} - 1}{e^{2z} + 1}\). Give 3 decimal places.
explanation: The exponent is \(2z\): double \(z\) first, then use the \(e^x\) key. \(e^{2z}\) is not \(e^2 \times z\). Work out \(e^{2z}\) once, then use it on both the top and the bottom of the fraction. The result must lie between \(-1\) and \(+1\).

prompt: In \(e_i = Y_i - \hat{Y}_i\), what is \(\hat{Y}_i\)?
choices: The value predicted by the regression line for individual \(i\) ;; The observed value for individual \(i\) ;; The mean of all the \(Y\) values ;; A transformed value of \(Y\)
explanation: A hat marks an estimate or prediction, as in \(\hat{p}\). \(\hat{Y}_i\) is where the line says individual \(i\) should be, given its \(X\). The residual \(e_i\) is the observed value minus the predicted one: how far the point sits above the line (positive) or below it (negative). This \(e_i\) has nothing to do with the number \(e \approx 2.718\).

prompt: A regression line is \(Y = {{a}} + {{b}}X\). For an individual with \(X = {{X}}\) and observed \(Y = {{Y}}\), calculate the predicted value \(\hat{Y}\) and the residual \(e = Y - \hat{Y}\).
data: a <- round(runif(1, 1, 10), 1); b <- round(runif(1, 0.5, 3), 2); X <- sample(2:15, 1); yhat <- a + b * X; Y <- round(yhat + sample(c(-1, 1), 1) * runif(1, 0.5, 3), 1)
explanation: \({{b}}X\) means \({{b}} \times X\): multiply first, then add the intercept. The residual is observed minus predicted, in that order; a negative residual means the point is below the line.

prompt: From a sample, \(S_{XY} = {{sxy}}\), \(SS_X = {{ssx}}\), \(\bar{X} = {{xbar}}\) and \(\bar{Y} = {{ybar}}\). Calculate the slope \(b = \dfrac{S_{XY}}{SS_X}\) and the intercept \(a = \bar{Y} - b\bar{X}\).
data: ssx <- sample(c(20, 40, 50, 80, 100), 1); b <- round(runif(1, 0.3, 2.5), 2); sxy <- round(b * ssx, 2); xbar <- round(runif(1, 5, 20), 1); ybar <- round(runif(1, 10, 40), 1)
explanation: Find \(b\) first, because \(a\) needs it. In \(a = \bar{Y} - b\bar{X}\), \(b\bar{X}\) is a product: multiply before subtracting. This formula guarantees that the line passes through the point \((\bar{X}, \bar{Y})\).
worked:
\(b = \dfrac{ {{sxy}} }{ {{ssx}} } = {{round(sxy / ssx, 4)}}\)
\(a = {{ybar}} - {{round(sxy / ssx, 4)}} \times {{xbar}} = {{ybar}} - {{round(sxy / ssx * xbar, 4)}} = {{round(ybar - sxy / ssx * xbar, 4)}}\)

prompt: A regression has slope \(b = {{b}}\), \(MS_{residual} = {{msr}}\) and \(\sum (X_i - \bar{X})^2 = {{ssx}}\). Calculate \(SE_b = \sqrt{\dfrac{MS_{residual}}{\sum (X_i - \bar{X})^2}}\), then \(t = \dfrac{b - \beta_0}{SE_b}\) for the null hypothesis \(\beta_0 = 0\). Give 3 decimal places for \(SE_b\) and 2 for \(t\).
data: msr <- round(runif(1, 2, 20), 2); ssx <- sample(c(50, 80, 120, 200, 400), 1); seb <- sqrt(msr / ssx); b <- round(runif(1, 1.5, 5) * seb, 3)
explanation: The square root covers the whole fraction: divide first, then take the root. \(\sum (X_i - \bar{X})^2\) is \(SS_X\) written out in full. \(\beta_0\) is the slope stated by the null hypothesis; when it is 0, \(t\) is simply \(b\) divided by its standard error.
rcode:
SE_b <- sqrt({{msr}} / {{ssx}})
SE_b
({{b}} - 0) / SE_b

prompt: A regression has \(SS_{residual} = {{ssr}}\) and \(SS_{total} = {{sst}}\). Calculate \(R^2 = 1 - \dfrac{SS_{residual}}{SS_{total}}\). Give 3 decimal places.
explanation: Divide first, then subtract the result from 1. The fraction is the share of variation the line leaves unexplained, so its complement is the share explained. For a regression with one predictor, \(R^2\) equals \(r^2\), the square of the correlation coefficient.

prompt: In Spearman's rank correlation, \(r_s = \dfrac{S_{RS}}{\sqrt{SS_R \cdot SS_S}}\). What are \(R\) and \(S\)?
choices: The ranks of the X values and the ranks of the Y values ;; Two rank sums, as in the Mann-Whitney U test ;; \(R\) is a row total and \(S\) is a standard deviation ;; \(R\) is \(R^2\) and \(S\) is the sum of products
explanation: Spearman's correlation is Pearson's formula with each value replaced by its rank: \(R\) for the ranks of X and \(S\) for the ranks of Y. Compare \(S_{RS}\) with \(S_{XY}\): the same structure with different letters. \(R\) has many other jobs (rank sums \(R_1\), row totals \(R_i\), \(R^2\)), so read it in context.

prompt: Using the excerpt below from a table of critical values for Spearman's rank correlation, find the critical value for \(\alpha = {{a}}\) (two-tailed) with \(n = {{n}}\).{{tab_spearman(n)}}
data: a <- sample(c(0.05, 0.05, 0.01), 1); j <- sample(which(spearman_tab$n >= 10), 1); n <- spearman_tab$n[j]; cv <- if (a == 0.05) spearman_tab$c05[j] else spearman_tab$c01[j]
explanation: This table is looked up by \(n\), the number of pairs, not by degrees of freedom; then use the column for \(\alpha = {{a}}\). If the size of your \(r_s\) (ignoring its sign) is greater than or equal to the critical value, \(P \leq {{a}}\). Larger samples need smaller correlations to be significant, which is why the critical values shrink as \(n\) grows, and a smaller \(\alpha\) needs a larger correlation.
rcode:
# There is no built-in function for this table.
# cor.test(x, y, method = "spearman") gives the P-value directly.

prompt: The standard error of a correlation coefficient is \(SE_r = \sqrt{\dfrac{1 - r^2}{n - 2}}\). What is it calculated from?
choices: Only \(r\) and the sample size \(n\) ;; The residuals from a fitted regression line ;; The standard deviations of X and Y ;; The sum of products \(S_{XY}\)
explanation: Everything in the formula is either \(r\) or \(n\). No line is fitted in a correlation analysis, so there are no residuals; residuals (observed minus predicted \(Y\)) belong to regression. A stronger correlation (\(r^2\) closer to 1) or a larger sample gives a smaller standard error. The divisor is \(n - 2\) because two means, of X and of Y, were estimated from the data.
rcode:
r <- 0.534; n <- 24
sqrt((1 - r^2) / (n - 2))   # needs only r and n

prompt: Earlier t statistics subtracted a null value, as in \(t = \dfrac{\bar{Y} - \mu_0}{SE_{\bar{Y}}}\). Why does the t statistic for a correlation, \(t = \dfrac{r}{SE_r}\), have no null value?
choices: The null hypothesis is \(\rho = 0\), and subtracting 0 changes nothing ;; A correlation has no null hypothesis ;; The null value is already built into \(SE_r\) ;; \(r\) is a population value, so nothing is subtracted
explanation: You can think of it as \(t = \dfrac{r - 0}{SE_r}\): the null hypothesis is that the population correlation \(\rho\) is 0, so the subtraction drops out. The same happens in \(t = \dfrac{b - \beta_0}{SE_b}\) when \(\beta_0 = 0\), and in the two-sample t-test when \((\mu_1 - \mu_2)_0 = 0\). This t-test only works for a null value of 0; testing any other value of \(\rho\) uses Fisher's \(z\) instead.

prompt: From a sample of \(n = {{n}}\) pairs, \(S_{XY} = {{sxy}}\) and \(SS_X = {{ssx}}\). Calculate the covariance \(Cov(X,Y) = \dfrac{S_{XY}}{n-1}\), the variance of X, \(s_X^2 = \dfrac{SS_X}{n-1}\), and then the slope \(b = \dfrac{Cov(X,Y)}{s_X^2}\). Give 3 decimal places.
data: n <- sample(8:20, 1); sxy <- round(runif(1, 20, 200), 1) * sample(c(1, 1, -1), 1); ssx <- round(runif(1, 40, 300), 1)
explanation: Covariance is built like a variance, but with the product of the X and Y deviations in place of a squared deviation, so it measures how X and Y change together. It is not the standard deviation of X. Dividing it by the variance of X gives the slope; the two \(n - 1\)'s cancel, which is why \(b = \dfrac{S_{XY}}{SS_X}\) gives the same answer. Dividing the covariance by both standard deviations instead gives \(r\).
rcode:
n <- {{n}}; Sxy <- {{sxy}}; SSx <- {{ssx}}
covXY <- Sxy / (n - 1); varX <- SSx / (n - 1)
covXY; varX
covXY / varX   # slope
Sxy / SSx      # the same
# with raw data: cov(X, Y) / var(X)

prompt: Hypothetical example. Body mass (g) is regressed on body length (cm), giving the slope \(b = {{b}}\) and the correlation \(r = {{r}}\). What are the units of \(b\) and \(r\)?
choices: \(b\) is in grams per centimetre; \(r\) has no units ;; Both are in grams per centimetre ;; \(b\) has no units; \(r\) is in grams per centimetre ;; \(b\) is in centimetres per gram; \(r\) is in grams
explanation: The slope is the change in Y for each one-unit change in X, so it carries the units of Y per unit of X: here, grams per centimetre. In \(b = \dfrac{S_{XY}}{SS_X}\), the top is in g \(\times\) cm and the bottom in cm \(\times\) cm, leaving g per cm. In \(r = \dfrac{S_{XY}}{\sqrt{SS_X \cdot SS_Y}}\), the units on the top and bottom cancel completely, which is why \(r\) always lies between \(-1\) and \(+1\), whatever the units.

prompt: Hypothetical example. After fit <- lm(age ~ black), coefficients(fit) prints (Intercept) {{a}} and black {{b}}. Which is the regression equation?
choices: Predicted age \(= {{a}} + {{b}} \times\) black ;; Predicted age \(= {{b}} + {{a}} \times\) black ;; Predicted black \(= {{a}} + {{b}} \times\) age ;; Predicted age \(= {{a}} \times {{b}} \times\) black
explanation: R lists the intercept first, labelled (Intercept), then one slope for each explanatory variable, labelled with that variable's name. In lm(age ~ black), the response is on the left of the ~ and the explanatory variable is on the right, so the line predicts age from black. To pull out one value, index the vector: coefficients(fit)[1] is the intercept and coefficients(fit)[2] is the slope. summary(fit) gives the same estimates with their standard errors.
rcode:
fit <- lm(age ~ black)
coefficients(fit)      # intercept first, then the slope
coefficients(fit)[2]   # just the slope

prompt: A regression line gives \(\hat{Y} = {{yh}}\) at \(X = {{x}}\), a value inside the range of X in the data. What does \(\hat{Y}\) estimate?
choices: The mean of Y for all individuals with \(X = {{x}}\) ;; The exact Y that every individual with \(X = {{x}}\) will have ;; The largest Y possible at \(X = {{x}}\) ;; The mean of all the Y values in the sample
explanation: A hat marks an estimate. \(\hat{Y}\) estimates the average Y for individuals with that X; some individuals lie above the line and some below, which is what the residuals measure. Make predictions only within the range of X in the data, because there is no way to know whether the relationship stays linear outside that range.
rcode:
# with fit <- lm(Y ~ X):
predict(fit, newdata = data.frame(X = {{x}}))

prompt: You calculate Spearman's \(r_s = {{rs}}\) from \(n = {{n}}\) pairs. Using the excerpt below from the table of critical values, what can you report?{{tab_spearman(n)}}
data: j <- sample(which(spearman_tab$n >= 10 & spearman_tab$n <= 40), 1); n <- spearman_tab$n[j]; c05 <- spearman_tab$c05[j]; c01 <- spearman_tab$c01[j]; labs <- c('\\(P \\lt 0.01\\): reject \\(H_0: \\rho_S = 0\\)', '\\(0.01 \\lt P \\lt 0.05\\): reject \\(H_0: \\rho_S = 0\\)', '\\(P \\gt 0.05\\): do not reject \\(H_0: \\rho_S = 0\\)'); idx <- sample(1:3, 1); lo <- c(c01 + 0.01, c05 + 0.01, 0.10)[idx]; hi <- c(0.95, c01 - 0.01, c05 - 0.01)[idx]; rs <- round(runif(1, lo, hi), 3) * sample(c(1, 1, -1), 1); ok <- labs[idx]; w <- labs[-idx]
explanation: Use the size of \(r_s\), ignoring its sign: \(|r_s| = {{abs(rs)}}\). In the row for \(n = {{n}}\), the critical values are {{c05}} (\(\alpha = 0.05\)) and {{c01}} (\(\alpha = 0.01\)). Decide at your chosen \(\alpha\) (usually 0.05) with the first column; the second column narrows down the P-value. A value at least as large as the 0.05 critical value means \(P \leq 0.05\), and one at least as large as the 0.01 critical value means \(P \leq 0.01\). So {{ok}}.
rcode:
# with raw data, R gives the P-value directly:
cor.test(x, y, method = "spearman")

prompt: From a sample of \(n = {{n}}\), \(SS_Y = {{ssy}}\), \(S_{XY} = {{sxy}}\) and the slope is \(b = {{b}}\). Calculate \(MS_{residual} = \dfrac{SS_Y - b \cdot S_{XY}}{n - 2}\). Give 3 decimal places.
data: n <- sample(10:30, 1); ssx <- round(runif(1, 20, 120), 1); ssy <- round(runif(1, 30, 300), 1); rr <- runif(1, 0.4, 0.9) * sample(c(1, -1), 1); sxy <- round(rr * sqrt(ssx * ssy), 2); b <- round(sxy / ssx, 3)
explanation: Multiply \(b \cdot S_{XY}\) first, subtract it from \(SS_Y\), then divide the whole top by \(n - 2\). \(b\) and \(S_{XY}\) always have the same sign, so the product is positive and the top shrinks. This shortcut gives the same answer as \(\dfrac{\sum (Y_i - \hat{Y}_i)^2}{n - 2}\) without working out every \(\hat{Y}_i\). The df are \(n - 2\) because the line needed two estimates, \(a\) and \(b\).
worked:
\(b \cdot S_{XY} = {{b}} \times {{sxy}} = {{round(b * sxy, 4)}}\)
\(MS_{residual} = \dfrac{ {{ssy}} - {{round(b * sxy, 4)}} }{ {{n}} - 2} = \dfrac{ {{round(ssy - b * sxy, 4)}} }{ {{n - 2}} } = {{round((ssy - b * sxy) / (n - 2), 4)}}\)

prompt: Hypothetical example. Tadpole growth is measured at three temperatures, and each temperature is tested once in each of five ponds (blocks). Which model statement is the null model for testing the effect of temperature?
choices: GROWTH = CONSTANT + BLOCK ;; GROWTH = CONSTANT + BLOCK + TEMPERATURE ;; GROWTH = CONSTANT + TEMPERATURE ;; GROWTH = CONSTANT
explanation: The null model contains everything except the term being tested. BLOCK is part of the design, so it stays in both models; only TEMPERATURE is added in the alternative model, GROWTH = CONSTANT + BLOCK + TEMPERATURE. The F test then asks whether adding that one term improves the fit.
rcode:
# with a data frame containing growth, block and temperature:
null_model <- lm(growth ~ block)
full_model <- lm(growth ~ block + temperature)
anova(null_model, full_model)   # does adding temperature improve the fit?

prompt: In the model statement RESPONSE = CONSTANT + A + B + A*B, what does A*B represent?
choices: The interaction: whether the effect of A depends on the level of B ;; Multiply the values of A and B together before fitting the model ;; A and B entered a second time, so they count twice ;; The total of the two main effects
explanation: Model statements are not arithmetic: the plus signs mean 'include this term', and A*B is the name of the interaction term. A and B on their own are the main effects. An interaction means the effect of one factor changes depending on the level of the other, so the lines on an interaction plot are not parallel. (In an R formula, A*B is shorthand for all three terms, A + B + A:B.)
rcode:
# with a data frame containing response, A and B:
lm(response ~ A + B + A:B)   # A:B is the interaction term
lm(response ~ A * B)         # shorthand for exactly the same model

prompt: In a model statement such as RESPONSE = CONSTANT + TREATMENT, what is CONSTANT?
choices: The baseline (a mean or an intercept): the starting value that the other terms adjust ;; A value that is the same for every treatment, so it can be ignored ;; The number of observations ;; The error, or residual, term
explanation: CONSTANT stands for the baseline that every prediction starts from: a mean in an ANOVA-type model, or the intercept in a regression-type model. Which mean depends on how the model is coded. Written as \(Y = \mu + A\), the constant is the grand mean and each group effect is a difference from it; in R's default output, the intercept is the mean of the reference group instead, and the other estimates are differences from that group. The predicted group means are the same either way; only the numbers attached to the terms change. The simplest possible model, RESPONSE = CONSTANT, predicts every observation with the same single value, the grand mean.
rcode:
# R includes the constant (intercept) automatically:
lm(response ~ treatment)
lm(response ~ 1 + treatment)   # the same model, constant written out

prompt: Which model statement describes a two-factor experiment that tests both factors and whether the effect of one factor depends on the other?
choices: RESPONSE = CONSTANT + A + B + A*B ;; RESPONSE = CONSTANT + A + B ;; RESPONSE = CONSTANT + A*B ;; RESPONSE = CONSTANT + BLOCK + A
explanation: 'Both factors' gives the two main effects, A and B; 'depends on the other' is the interaction, A*B. Leaving out A*B assumes the two effects simply add together. An interaction is normally fitted together with its main effects, not on its own.
rcode: lm(response ~ A * B)   # A, B and the A:B interaction

prompt: A multiple regression with \(p = {{p}}\) predictors and \(n = {{n}}\) observations has \(R^2 = {{R2}}\). Calculate \(R_{adj}^2 = 1 - (1 - R^2)(n - 1)/(n - p - 1)\). Give 3 decimal places.
explanation: Work out the three brackets first: \(1 - R^2\), \(n - 1\) and \(n - p - 1\). Multiply the first two, divide by the third, and subtract the result from 1 last. \(R_{adj}^2\) is always a little smaller than \(R^2\), because it is penalised for each extra predictor.

choices: The number of predictor variables, not counting the intercept ;; The proportion of variation explained ;; The P-value of the model ;; The number of parameters, including the intercept
explanation: The letter \(p\) has many jobs in statistics: a proportion, the P-value (usually a capital \(P\)), and here a count of predictors. Read it in its own formula. With one predictor, \(p = 1\) and the denominator becomes \(n - 2\), the same df as in a simple regression.

prompt: Hypothetical example. The model DIVERSITY = CONSTANT + BLOCK + TREATMENT gives these estimates: Intercept (Block 1, Control) \(= {{int}}\); Block {{blk}} \(= {{bk}}\); Treatment High \(= {{tr}}\). What is the predicted diversity for the High treatment in Block {{blk}}?
data: int <- round(runif(1, 2, 6), 2); bk <- round(runif(1, -1.2, 0.8), 2); tr <- round(runif(1, -2, 1.5), 2); blk <- sample(2:5, 1)
explanation: In R's default coding, the intercept is the prediction for the reference levels, here Block 1 and Control. Every other estimate is an adjustment from there, so add the ones that apply: the block's and the treatment's. A negative estimate lowers the prediction. A level that does not appear in the list is the reference level, with an adjustment of 0.

prompt: A design principle says that, for a fixed total sample size, the standard error of a difference is smallest when \(|n_1 - n_2| = 0\). What does \(|n_1 - n_2| = 0\) mean?
choices: The two groups are the same size ;; Group 1 is larger than group 2 ;; Both groups are empty ;; The groups differ in size, but the sign of the difference does not matter
explanation: The bars give the size of the difference, ignoring its sign. The only way for that size to be 0 is \(n_1 = n_2\): a balanced design. For example, with 20 individuals, splitting them 10 and 10 gives a smaller \(\sqrt{\frac{1}{n_1} + \frac{1}{n_2}}\) (0.447) than splitting them 5 and 15 (0.516).

prompt: To plan a two-sample study with power 0.8, use \(n = 16\left(\dfrac{\sigma}{D}\right)^2\), where \(D = |\mu_1 - \mu_2|\) is the difference of interest. With \(\sigma = {{sig}}\) and \(D = {{D}}\), how many individuals are needed in each group? Round up to a whole number.
explanation: Divide first, then square the result, then multiply by 16. The square applies to the whole fraction \(\frac{\sigma}{D}\), not just to \(\sigma\). Always round sample sizes up: you cannot study part of an individual, and rounding down would leave you short of the target power. Halving \(D\) quadruples the sample size, because of the square.
worked: \(n = 16 \times \left(\dfrac{ {{sig}} }{ {{D}} }\right)^2 = 16 \times {{round(sig / D, 4)}}^2 = 16 \times {{round((sig / D)^2, 4)}} = {{round(16 * (sig / D)^2, 4)}}\), which rounds up to {{ceiling(round(16 * (sig / D)^2, 6))}}
rcode:
16 * ({{sig}} / {{D}})^2
ceiling(16 * ({{sig}} / {{D}})^2)   # always round up

prompt: To plan a study for a chosen precision, use \(n = 8\left(\dfrac{\sigma}{\text{margin of error}}\right)^2\). With \(\sigma = {{sig}}\) and a desired margin of error of {{me}}, how many individuals are needed in each group? Round up to a whole number.
explanation: Same structure as the power formula: divide inside the brackets, square, then multiply by 8. Round up, never down. Asking for a margin of error half as large needs four times as many individuals.
worked: \(n = 8 \times \left(\dfrac{ {{sig}} }{ {{me}} }\right)^2 = 8 \times {{round((sig / me)^2, 4)}} = {{round(8 * (sig / me)^2, 4)}}\), which rounds up to {{ceiling(round(8 * (sig / me)^2, 6))}}
rcode:
8 * ({{sig}} / {{me}})^2
ceiling(8 * ({{sig}} / {{me}})^2)   # always round up

prompt: Two groups have means \(\bar{Y}_1 = {{y1}}\) and \(\bar{Y}_2 = {{y2}}\), with pooled standard deviation \(s_{pooled} = {{sp}}\). Calculate Cohen's \(d = \dfrac{\bar{Y}_1 - \bar{Y}_2}{s_{pooled}}\). Give 2 decimal places.
data: y1 <- round(runif(1, 20, 40), 1); sp <- round(runif(1, 2, 6), 1); y2 <- round(y1 - runif(1, 0.3, 1.5) * sp, 1)
explanation: Subtract on top first, then divide by the pooled standard deviation: not the variance \(s_p^2\), and not a standard error. Cohen's \(d\) expresses the difference in standard-deviation units, so it does not depend on sample size. This \(d\) is unrelated to the paired difference \(d\) in a paired t-test.

prompt: A study is designed to have power \(= {{pw}}\). Using \(Power = 1 - \beta\), what is \(\beta\), the Type II error rate?
explanation: Rearranging \(Power = 1 - \beta\) gives \(\beta = 1 - Power\). Power is the probability of detecting a real effect and \(\beta\) is the probability of missing it, so the two add to 1. Do not mix up \(\beta\) with \(\alpha\), the Type I error rate, which is set separately (often 0.05).

prompt: True or false: the \(\beta\) in 'confidence interval for \(\beta = b \pm t_{\alpha(2),df} \cdot SE_b\)' and the \(\beta\) in '\(Power = 1 - \beta\)' mean the same thing.
explanation: The first \(\beta\) is the population slope, which \(b\) estimates; Greek letters stand for population values. The second is the Type II error rate. It is the same letter with two unrelated jobs, so read \(\beta\) in the formula it sits in.

prompt: You have \(N = {{N}}\) individuals to split between two groups. Using \(SE_{\bar{Y}_1 - \bar{Y}_2} \sim \sqrt{\dfrac{1}{n_1} + \dfrac{1}{n_2}}\), which split gives the smallest standard error?
explanation: \(\frac{1}{n}\) gets large quickly when \(n\) is small, so a lopsided split is dominated by its smaller group. Equal groups, \(|n_1 - n_2| = 0\), make the sum of the two fractions as small as possible. For example, \(\frac{1}{ {{h}} } + \frac{1}{ {{h}} } = {{round(2 / h, 3)}}\), but \(\frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{ {{N - 2}} } = {{round(0.5 + 1 / (N - 2), 3)}}\).
rcode:
n1 <- c({{h}}, {{h - 4}}, {{N / 5}}, 2)
n2 <- {{N}} - n1
sqrt(1 / n1 + 1 / n2)   # smallest for the equal split

prompt: Hypothetical example. The response values are \(Y = \lbrace {{lst(Y)}} \rbrace\). What is the intercept (the CONSTANT) of the null model, lm(Y ~ 1)? Give 2 decimal places.
explanation: In an R formula, 1 means 'include an intercept'. A model with only the intercept predicts the same value for every observation, and that value is the mean, so the intercept of the null model is the grand mean of \(Y\). R includes an intercept automatically, so lm(Y ~ X + 1) is the same model as lm(Y ~ X). Once a term is added, the intercept means something else (where the line crosses \(X = 0\), or the mean of the reference group), even though R still labels it (Intercept).
rcode:
Y <- c({{lst(Y)}})
coef(lm(Y ~ 1))   # the intercept of the null model
mean(Y)           # the same number

prompt: In the one-factor linear model \(\hat{Y} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 G_2 + \beta_2 G_3 + \beta_3 G_4\), what is \(G_3\)?
choices: An indicator: 1 for individuals in group 3 and 0 for everyone else ;; The mean of group 3 ;; The number of individuals in group 3 ;; The difference between the mean of group 3 and the mean of group 1
explanation: The G terms are 0/1 switches, like an if-statement: \(G_3\) switches \(\beta_2\) on for individuals in group 3 and off for everyone else. \(\beta_0\) has no G because every prediction starts from it. In R's default coding, \(\beta_0\) is the mean of the reference group (group 1), and each of the other \(\beta\)'s is a difference from that mean, so a negative \(\beta\) means the group's mean is below the reference group's. R picks the reference group alphabetically unless told otherwise. A different coding (for example, a grand-mean baseline) or a different reference group changes the \(\beta\)'s, but not the G's and not the predicted group means.

prompt: In \(\hat{Y} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 G_2 + \beta_2 G_3 + \beta_3 G_4\), R's output (default coding, group 1 as the reference group) gives \(\beta_0 = {{b0}}\), \(\beta_1 = {{bs[1]}}\), \(\beta_2 = {{bs[2]}}\) and \(\beta_3 = {{bs[3]}}\). Calculate the predicted mean for group 1 and for group {{g}}.
explanation: Group 1 is the reference group: all the G's are 0, so its predicted mean is just \(\beta_0\). For group {{g}}, only \(G_{ {{g}} }\) is 1, so add the \(\beta\) it multiplies, \(\beta_{ {{g - 1}} }\), to \(\beta_0\). Notice that the subscripts are offset by one: \(\beta_1\) goes with \(G_2\), because group 1 has no G of its own. A negative \(\beta\) lowers the prediction below the reference group's mean. These \(\beta\)'s are estimates from the sample (some books write \(\hat{\beta}\) or \(b\) for them). Choosing a different reference group, or a different coding, would give different \(\beta\)'s but exactly the same predicted group means.

prompt: Hypothetical example. Plant growth is measured under three fertiliser treatments (none, low and high), and every treatment is used once in each of five fields (blocks). Which statement is correct?
choices: 'None' is the control, one level of the treatment; the fields are blocks, whose differences the design accounts for ;; The blocks are the control groups ;; There are 15 treatment levels, one for each plot ;; A block is removed from the model if it is not significant
explanation: A control is one level of the treatment being tested; in R it is usually the reference level that the other levels are compared with. A block groups plots that share conditions the researcher cannot control, such as soil or drainage. Putting every treatment in every block lets the model account for that variation. A block stays in the model whether or not it is significant, because it is part of the design.
rcode: lm(growth ~ block + fertiliser)   # the block is part of the design: it stays in

prompt: Hypothetical example. In a data frame, the five blocks are coded as the numbers 1 to 5. What should you do before fitting lm(growth ~ block + fertiliser)?
choices: Convert block with factor(), so that R fits a separate effect for each block ;; Nothing: R treats any column of numbers as groups ;; Remove block from the model, because numbers cannot be blocks ;; Write block*fertiliser instead
explanation: If block is stored as numbers, R treats it as a numerical variable and fits a single slope for it, as if block 5 were five times block 1. factor() tells R that the numbers are only labels for groups, so each block gets its own effect. str() shows how a column is stored: a factor is listed as Factor, and a numeric column as num or int.
rcode:
dat$block <- factor(dat$block)   # labels, not quantities
str(dat)                         # block should now be a Factor
lm(growth ~ block + fertiliser, data = dat)

prompt: True or false: adding another predictor to a multiple regression can make \(R^2\) smaller.
explanation: \(R^2 = 1 - \dfrac{SS_{residual}}{SS_{total}}\), and each new predictor removes at least a little variation from \(SS_{residual}\), even a predictor unrelated to Y. So \(R^2\) never goes down as predictors are added, and a higher \(R^2\) alone is no reason to keep a predictor. \(R_{adj}^2\) penalises each extra predictor, so it can go down; it is used in every multiple regression, whether or not the predictors are correlated.

prompt: Hypothetical example. A multiple regression of seedling height on light and water gives \(P = {{p1}}\) for light and \(P = {{p2}}\) for water. What do these two P-values test?
choices: Each tests its own null hypothesis: that this predictor has no relationship with height (a slope of 0) ;; Whether light is a better predictor than water ;; Whether the light and water slopes are equal ;; The smaller P-value shows which predictor is more important
explanation: Each P-value belongs to its own term and tests whether that term improves the fit: whether its slope differs from 0, a flat line. Neither one compares the predictors with each other, so P-values of different terms should not be compared to decide which predictor matters more. Here both are below 0.05, so both predictors stay in the model.

prompt: Hypothetical example. In a regression with three predictors, one predictor is not significant. Which equation should you report?
choices: Refit the model without that predictor, and use the new coefficients ;; Use the three-predictor equation, and leave out the non-significant term ;; Use the three-predictor equation unchanged ;; Fit each predictor in its own simple regression, and combine the slopes
explanation: The coefficients depend on which other predictors are in the model, because correlated predictors share some of the same explained variation. So after dropping a term, fit the simpler model again and use its coefficients. Each coefficient is a partial regression coefficient: the change in predicted Y per unit of that predictor while the other predictors are held constant.
rcode:
lm1 <- lm(y ~ x1 + x2 + x3)
lm2 <- lm(y ~ x1 + x2)   # refit without x3
coef(lm2)                # use these coefficients

prompt: In a two-factor ANOVA, the interaction A*B is significant. How should you interpret the main effect of A?
choices: With caution: the effect of A depends on the level of B, so describe the interaction first, using a plot of the means ;; Ignore the interaction, because the main effect is what was tested ;; Remove A from the model, because only the interaction matters ;; The main effect of A is the same at every level of B
explanation: A main effect is the difference between the levels of A, averaged over the levels of B. When A and B interact, the lines on an interaction plot are not parallel, so that average can mislead: it may come from only one level of B, or crossing lines can hide a real effect. Look at the interaction first, and if it is significant, build the conclusion around how the effect of A changes with B. No P-value cut-off decides this; the plot of the means shows whether the effect holds at every level of B. An interaction is normally kept together with its main effects.

prompt: True or false: if every term in a model has \(P \lt 0.05\), the model must explain most of the variation in Y.
explanation: A small P-value says an effect is unlikely to be due to chance alone; it does not say the effect is large or that the model fits closely. Check \(R^2 = 1 - \dfrac{SS_{residual}}{SS_{total}}\): with highly variable data, significant terms can still leave most of the variation unexplained. For example, \(R^2 = 0.23\) leaves 77% of the variation unexplained.

prompt: The model RESPONSE = CONSTANT + A + B has \(MS_A = {{msa}}\), \(MS_B = {{msb}}\) and \(MS_{residual} = {{msr}}\), with \(df_{residual} = {{dfr}}\). Each term has 1 df. Calculate \(F_A = \dfrac{MS_A}{MS_{residual}}\) and \(F_B = \dfrac{MS_B}{MS_{residual}}\), and find the critical value they are compared with, \(F_{0.05(1), 1, {{dfr}} }\), from the excerpt of the F table below. Give 2 decimal places.{{tab_f(1, dfr)}}
answer_expr: c(msa / msr, msb / msr, round(qf(0.95, 1, dfr), 2))
explanation: Each F-ratio divides that term's mean square by the same \(MS_{residual}\), so terms with the same numerator df are compared with the same critical value, \(F_{0.05(1), 1, {{dfr}} }\). The second df always comes from the residual. If an interaction term with 1 df were added to the model, \(df_{residual}\) would drop to {{dfr - 1}}, and every term would then be compared with \(F_{0.05(1), 1, {{dfr - 1}} }\).
